title: Bengaluru Startup's Hospital Music Night Sparks Backlash — and a Sequel
excerpt: Superhealth founder Varun Dubey defended the August event as an attempt to build 'hospitals that don't scare people'; weeks later he announced a 'Bhajan Jam' at the same hospital.
body:
• Superhealth Hospitals, a Bengaluru healthcare startup, hosted a "music night" inside one of its hospitals in late August; videos of the event went viral and drew sharp online criticism as insensitive.
  • Founder and CEO Varun Dubey defended the event on X, saying the hospital's outpatient departments had closed at 8 pm, the event started at 10 pm, and only non-clinical floors were used — arguing hospitals should not be places of fear and gloom.
  • Weeks later, Dubey doubled down with a sequel: a "Bhajan Jam" at the same hospital, announced with a dig at critics — "After the 'rave' reception…We're back."
  • The episode has reignited a wider debate about whether India's hospitals can be made warmer and less intimidating without trivializing the seriousness of healthcare.

When videos surfaced last month showing a musical evening with guests, lights and sound inside a working hospital in Bengaluru, the reaction was swift and severe. The event had been organized by Superhealth Hospitals, a startup founded to rebuild Indian healthcare around fixed pricing and zero wait times. The Independent was among the outlets that covered the story as the backlash mounted — commentators called the party insensitive to patients and families grappling with illness inside the same building.

The defense came from the top. Varun Dubey, Superhealth's founder and CEO, took to X to argue that the event had been carefully thought through — and that hospitals themselves are overdue for a rethink.

What actually happened inside the hospital

According to Dubey's post on X, reported by Mint, the hospital's outpatient departments had shut by 8 pm and the musical event began at 10 pm. Registration was carried out in the OPD lobby, but the main event was confined to the basement, mezzanine and fourth floor, which houses the company's office. Clinical areas were off-limits.

Dubey said the guest list had been carefully curated and that patients and their attendants were welcome to attend. According to him, some patients and attendants joined simply to escape boredom, seek a distraction, or spend time in an environment that felt less lonely.

He acknowledged the optics head-on. "This Saturday night, we tried something unusual: we hosted a musical event at the hospital. I know how that sounds a little WTF. And plenty of people have been outraged by it. But hear me out," he wrote.

"Superhealth was founded with the aim of building hospitals that don't scare people."

— Varun Dubey, founder and CEO of Superhealth Hospitals

Why the backlash stung

The criticism cut deeper than one evening of music. Commenters described the event as a "rave" inside a place of suffering, and some questioned whether a hospital — where families wait on test results and grieve — could ever be an appropriate venue for a party. A YouTube news explainer on the controversy framed the tension precisely: organizers said the aim was to make hospitals feel less intimidating, while critics asked whether warmth could come at the cost of patient sensitivity, privacy and the seriousness of healthcare spaces.

Dubey, a veteran of India's healthcare and startup worlds who previously served as chief revenue officer at Apollo Hospitals and CMO at Ola Electric and Practo, is building Superhealth as a direct challenge to the country's hospital business model — salaried doctors with no commissions, fixed all-inclusive pricing, and zero wait times. The company says 50,000 subscribers collectively saved over ₹200 crore in healthcare spending in its first six months of operation. That reformist brand made the misstep more visible: a startup preaching radically honest healthcare had to answer for a party in a hospital.

The diaspora angle

For Indians abroad, hospital visits back home are often one of the most stressful parts of family emergencies — the crowds, the opacity of billing, the fear-laden corridors. Dubey's core thesis, that hospitals need not be morose and frightening, will resonate with anyone who has navigated a loved one's care in India. The controversy, though, is a cautionary tale: the diaspora has seen how quickly good intentions around "experience" can read as tone-deaf when they collide with grief. The line between humanizing healthcare and trivializing it is one every hospital reformer — in India or anywhere — will have to walk carefully.

What's next: a 'Bhajan Jam'

Dubey has not backed down. Roughly four weeks after the first event, he announced a sequel at the same hospital — a "Bhajan Jam," a devotional music gathering — and took a public dig at his critics in the process.

"After the 'rave' reception…We're back with...a 'Bhajan Jam.'"

— Varun Dubey, founder and CEO of Superhealth Hospitals, on X

The choice of a bhajan — devotional rather than party music — reads as a deliberate answer to the criticism: this time the music is sacred, communal and culturally unassailable. Whether it defuses the controversy or simply restages it will become clear when the event happens. Either way, Superhealth has turned a PR crisis into a running experiment in hospital culture, and the rest of India's healthcare industry is watching to see whether "hospitals that don't scare people" becomes a movement — or a warning.
image_caption: Varun Dubey, founder and CEO of Superhealth Hospitals. Dubey publicly defended his startup after videos of a music night hosted inside its Bengaluru hospital drew online criticism last month.
